idiom_name: is declaration pattern (if (o is IFlushable f)) and as with a null test
implementation_notes: C#'s type-testing operators are the capability query: the is operator checks whether the run-time type is compatible with a type or interface and, with a declaration pattern, binds the handle in the same expression - `if (o is IFlushable f) f.Flush();` - while the as operator returns null instead of throwing when the conversion cannot be made (reference and nullable value types only). What replaces the classic structure is this operator pair: there is no cross-cast, because the interfaces a runtime type implements are part of its contract, and the compiler scopes the bound variable to the branch where the test succeeded. The reflective form (Type.IsAssignableFrom, Type.IsInstanceOfType) stays justified when the capability type is itself a runtime Type token inside a framework, but it is far slower than is/as.
pitfalls: as never throws, so a skipped null test turns a missing capability into a NullReferenceException at the next line; only the is declaration pattern makes the negative branch explicit.
is matches base types and interfaces, never exact type identity: use o.GetType() == typeof(T) only when provenance, not capability, is the question.

An explicitly implemented interface member (void IFlushable.Flush()) is not visible as a public method on the class, so a capability test can succeed where a duck-typed call would fail - that is the point of the interface, but it also means the type must declare it.
Reflection-based tests (IsAssignableFrom/IsInstanceOfType) are orders of magnitude slower than is/as and can break under trimming or AOT publishing, where reflection metadata may be removed.
